html:
The morning was warm when I left home. Under the bluest of skies, I was driven to Lisbon’s airport, where I bid my parents farewell. It was a departure that I imagined as a pause in our ongoing conversation rather than its reconfiguration. Hours later, as I stepped out of what was then Berlin’s Tegel airport, the first thing that struck me was the cold wind shallowing my breath. I had to go back inside and add layers I hadn’t imagined needing so soon. I relive that day often.

That day I crossed the city three times. I almost strayed on my way to the only place I knew: the university in Dahlem, where I would start my five-month Erasmus semester (an EU student-exchange programme). Waiting for the underground, I was taken by a language school advertisement at Samariterstraße, which asked: ‘Tired of speaking silly German?’ – a provocation that would imprint itself on me for years. Enthralled, I passed through streets that seemed unreal and insubstantial, as if venturing through a sea of meanings that meant nothing to me yet. I obsess over that day often.

I had read the Berlin sociologist Georg Simmel’s reflections about how the metropolis affects its dwellers, creating a certain ‘indifference toward the distinctions between things.’ This is a kind of protective numbness, an emotional flatness of the overstimulated urban denizen. More than a century ago, in this same city, he had named such numbness ‘the blasé’.

If the blasé, however, is overstimulated by familiarity, I was overstimulated by novelty. The novelty of a perceptual greyness. For the blasé, everything has been felt too often. For me, nothing had been felt at all. It wasn’t that I had become numb to distinctions between things; it was that I couldn’t perceive any distinctions at all. Meaning had not yet sedimented, no attachments had been formed. The cobbles would need to be well-trodden before they would tell me their stories. So, in time, I too would become indifferent.

How then do you compose meaning in a place that seems to refuse it? How do you become blasé in the place of arrival? And what about that place once called home?

In bars, waving my glass around, I would speak of these topics. I wanted to hear stories I hadn’t heard before. What about the others, my fellow travellers, who settled for unsettledness? I sought willing storytellers, other Portuguese migrants residing in Berlin. Across 2024 and 2025, I sat in cafés, kitchens, parks and bars where winding conversations returned textures of belonging. I asked few direct questions, in the hope that stories would find themselves.

I think of a moment from an interview with a girl who told me how, on one of her visits back to Portugal, her father, his eyes bright with welcome, asked if she was glad to once again sleep in her own childhood bed. She stuttered. One’s bed is usually at home. She understood the unsaid, the premise hidden behind her father’s loving eyes. And yet, when she thought about the bed she would like to sink into after a long trip, it was not that childhood bed she thought of. Instead, a riving sense of home was her answer.

Belonging, that elusive feeling, cannot simply bloom out of nowhere

This misalignment between parent and child, between what home means to those who stayed and what it means to those who left, is felt but seldom acknowledged. Maybe the people who love us most are often the least equipped to see what departure has done. Seeing it would mean accepting that we are no longer fully theirs, nor they fully ours. Home might be somewhere else now; it seems kinder simply not to point it out.

Home is not simply a matter of being in a place; it requires an entire world to be built, embodied, maintained. It is a peculiar way the body attunes itself to what’s at hand. Belonging, that elusive feeling, cannot simply bloom out of nowhere. It requires time and closeness to endow your world with meaning.

Somewhere in Berlin, there is a daughter with a bed she seldom thinks about. She notices it only from afar. Such is the quieter thing beneath Simmel’s numbness. The blasé’s indifference is not the absence of meaning, but its sediment. You grow numb to what you have thoroughly absorbed. To feel at home somewhere is to have earned the right to stop noticing it. This, perhaps, is how meaning is composed in a place that first refuses it. The blasé, then, might not be the opposite of belonging, but its symptom.

The first days can be the hardest. Grey skies, cutting cold. The weather appears as more than meteorology; it registers as a reminder that you are from elsewhere, that here even the sun seems to remind you of your strangeness. You look around, and others seem unaffected. ‘What am I doing here?’ becomes a refrain.

Unlike the cutting wind, there are changes that arrive gently, rehearsed before the greater drama. An exchange programme, perhaps, or a temporary job posting. Through promises of an escape from routine, departure seems a suspension rather than the story itself. You have institutional scaffolding and, most importantly, an end date. There will be a return, you tell yourself. But departure also begins the subtle labour of reconfiguration. The realisation that the first day of the next five months might have been the first day of the rest of your life.

Berlin had gifted Simmel more than the blasé. In the same streets I now inhabit, he observed another figure. The stranger occupies a more unsettling position. They are not simply the other, the foreigner looking in, but someone who is neither entirely ‘them’ nor entirely ‘us’. Someone familiar to the very spaces that make for their strangeness. To be a stranger is to be in medias res, obliged to feel at ease in a story that has already started.

Both of Simmel’s figures share something. They make for a dual condition. The unbothered blasé and the unsettled stranger are entangled in their need for familiarity. The blasé can only grow numb to what they have already absorbed. The stranger can only be strange to places they have come to know.

What should feel most stable may erode precisely when it’s reached for

What I didn’t understand then was that becoming a stranger is not a moment, but a process. What starts as a temporary detour ends up reorienting an entire cartography of possibilities. The body that returns, even from these limited departures, is not the same one that left. A slow unfolding arises the instant you step away from familiar rhythms. The migrant will not tread out of the airport a stranger; they become one, grain by grain, through the accumulated weight of the everyday’s pulse. That strangeness, however, is not confined to the new. It finds its way back, even to that place once called home.

Departure transforms perception itself. It means not merely learning new rules, but feeling differently, altering what appears meaningful, close or distant. This altered perception doesn’t overlay the old. It retroactively changes how the once-familiar appears. Whatever introduces strangeness here will do the same there. Simmel’s own last years were spent away from Berlin. His writings on the stranger predate that departure. I wonder what he would have added had he returned.

Returning ‘home’ for a visit is walking ghostly paths. Not wholly yours, just familiar. ‘Every time I go back,’ someone told me, ‘the whole process feels like small bouts of grief.’ You will tread old, acquainted streets as a testimony of change. Once the initial commotion eases, once routine reasserts itself, there comes a feeling that it is time to leave again. The feeling settles in that home is not fully there anymore. And yet it will always be. Grieving for a loss that can only be felt, never quite named. Stranger in the place of departure than in the place of arrival.

The stranger has often been evoked in the third person; rarely is the writer included in this strangeness. And rarely does the figure account for what happens upon return. But the stranger must have left somewhere. Strangeness then is not directional; it is recursive. It folds back upon itself. It makes us exiles from a former self. What should feel most stable may erode precisely when it’s reached for. Home is not something to simply return to. Such is a peculiar arithmetic of departure.

On one of those grey, wintry days that Berlin so generously offers, sitting in someone’s kitchen, I heard the remark: ‘I used to think a lot about what I could gain here, and I’ve gained, I’d say, but I hadn’t realised so much what I could lose, you know?’ These words brought up something in me. In that kitchen, I thought of how, with time, something had also shifted in me. A form of change that didn’t announce itself, that went years unnoticed, yet continuously accruing. Not a crisis, but a silent drift. A misalignment between the stories I tell myself and the body I feel. I’ve come to call it unbecoming: a tension between a lived self and its socially recognisable articulation. It doesn’t demand resolution, yet becomes noticeable in moments of hesitation. A tacit detachment from who I expect myself to be. A reaching for words that don’t quite fit, yet no better alternative presents itself.

To unbecome is not to come undone. It is the accretive awareness that something no longer fits as before. It is to feel the weight of change before one has the words for it. A transformation so gradual that you notice it only when standing at the place of departure, only to find that it, like you, has become something stranger than you remembered. It is neither tragedy nor triumph.

The sigh that follows so many failed attempts at articulating this says what words alone cannot

Others recognised this feeling. A stranger might feel more like themselves in their new milieu than they ever did at ‘home’. They nevertheless miss a version of themselves who existed only there. This gap between what is felt and what can be said is itself a measure of change. And these are stories of change, after all.

The sigh that follows so many failed attempts at articulating this says what words alone cannot. How do you paint the picture of who you see yourself to be when the very feelings contest the words available? Loss is not the opposite of gain, but is somehow produced by it. Every new capacity for feeling at home in the place of arrival might also be a small chipping away at the ability to feel at home in the place of departure. What if, at a distance, becoming implies a quiet unbecoming? A strange resolution for a strange arithmetic.

The morning was warm when I left home. What was supposed to be a short five-month stay will soon be nine years. Yet the bluest of skies still has a hold on me. What in the moment felt like the most ordinary of days is now a refrain. I relive that day often. On returning, I’m left with questions that seem to resist resolution altogether. Maybe this too is recursive. How could it ever be anything but?

Yet the bluest of skies does not soothe the strangest of feelings.
